children: By Ed Frankl
The AI investment boom has lifted the British economy, underlining the technology's potential to drive growth beyond the U.S. and east Asia.

AI-related spending contributed as much as a third of  growth in the first seven months of the year, helped in particular by a jump in computer consultancy services, according to analysis by Deutsche Bank economists.

If sustained, the boost from AI could help the U.K. economy emerge from a long period of sluggish growth, and make it easier for the government to reduce its large debts. But for that to happen, economists say the technology would have to diffuse throughout the large services sector and boost productivity, a development that is by no means certain.

"Last year there was about 50 billion-60 billion pounds of announced investment in AI in the U.K. It didn't show up in the data much in 2025, but you're starting to see that filter through finally into the data this year," the bank's chief U.K. economist Sanjay Raja said.

Gross domestic product growth was 0.1% on month in August, latest official data from the U.K.'s statistics agency showed Thursday. That came after GDP expanded around 1.2% in the first half of the year, outpacing the U.S. and offsetting the worst fears that the war in Iran would hit the U.K. hard.

In the three months to August, GDP grew by 1.8% compared with June-August a year ago, the data showed. The sectors that contributed most to the pickup were professional, scientific and technical activities, alongside information and communication.
"Big picture, there are genuine tailwinds lifting the U.K. economy," Raja added.

Economies worldwide have proved more resilient than expected to the energy-price shock stemming from the war in the Middle East. The U.S. and China lead the way in capital expenditure on innovation and frontier models, with AI tech-investment rollout accounting for a third of U.S. economic growth in 2026, ING economists said in August.

The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday raised its forecast for Britain's full-year growth to 1.3%, among the largest upward revisions of any developed nation. But higher energy prices and long-term interest rates would weigh on U.K. consumption and investment next year, it noted.

Britain's economy has grown only sluggishly since the 2008 financial crisis, with relatively lackluster productivity exacerbated by high energy prices following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the downtrend in foreign investment after the U.K.'s exit from the European Union.

On the brighter side, economists point to the U.K.'s skilled talent base, top-tier universities and venture capital money flowing through London's financial district as reasons to see the country as a fertile ground for AI.
"The U.K. is certainly number one in Europe when it comes to funding of artificial intelligence and tech startups," Deutsche Bank's Raja said.

Spending in I.T. and AI-related industries contributed around 65% of business investment in the U.K. in the second quarter, Barclays economists said in a report. That incorporates software, hardware and infrastructure including data centers.
"This is, on a smaller scale, akin to what has been seen in the U.S. in recent years," report authors Jack Meaning and Cian Hennigan wrote.

Europe's largest cluster of data centers is in Slough, a town 25 miles west of London, with only Virginia in the U.S. boasting more globally. Earlier this year, U.S. logistics firm Prologis agreed to buy U.K. rival Segro, the parent company of Slough's trading estate that has benefited from the data-center build-out, for $19 billion.
Still, for AI to deliver a longer-term boost to growth,  building data centers won't be enough. Diffusion through the economy in a way that lifts productivity is key.

The U.K. remains attractive for firms looking to develop and deploy AI, with fairly light regulators and open capital markets, Kallum Pickering, chief economist at broker Peel Hunt, said. The big hurdle, however, is energy.
"Our ability to not just do the same things that we were doing before, but with AI to actually scale the economy using this technology--to grow the pie--is constrained by our energy policy," he said.

Governments need to throw their legislative weight behind speedy rollouts of more energy capacity for electricity-hungry AI technology, with Britain having some of the highest electricity prices in the advanced world,  he added.
Opportunities could also come as the EU moves forward with landmark AI regulation, when the U.K. has approached the subject more cautiously.
